name: Battle of Warsaw (1920)
info: In August 1920, during the Polish–Soviet War, a Polish counterattack under Józef Piłsudski broke Mikhail Tukhachevsky's Red Army advance on Warsaw and drove it eastward, and a treaty in 1921 fixed Poland's eastern frontier.

facts.date: August 1920: the final Soviet assault on Warsaw began on 12 August and the Polish counterattack from the south on 16 August; organised Soviet resistance had ceased by 21 August
facts.place: Warsaw and the country around it, including Radzymin, the Modlin Fortress, the Wkra River and the Vistula–Wieprz area to the south, in present-day Poland
facts.sides: Poland under Józef Piłsudski, with 32 divisions, 46,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry in the Polish order of battle; Soviet Russia's Western Front under Mikhail Tukhachevsky, with 24 divisions in four armies
facts.outcome: The Polish counterattack disrupted the Soviet offensive and forced the Red Army into a disorganised withdrawal eastward. Three of the four Soviet armies of the North-Western Front all but disintegrated.

t: Piłsudski drew up his plan on the night of 5 to 6 August 1920 and gathered a Task Force of about 20,000 men in the south, a plan many senior officers and French advisers called amateurish and Piłsudski himself called a gamble.
On the first day of the counteroffensive, 16 August, four of five Polish divisions advanced 45 kilometres north without opposition into the gap between the two Soviet fronts.
Red Army losses are put at about 15,000 dead, 500 missing, 10,000 wounded and 65,000 captured, against Polish losses of approximately 4,500 killed, 22,000 wounded and 10,000 missing.
dyk: To stop the one Soviet radio station of the 4th Army that was still working, Polish operators in Warsaw recited the Book of Genesis in Polish and Latin on its frequency, so that it lost contact with its headquarters.
ev: Semyon Budyonny's 1st Cavalry Army breaks through the Polish lines and all Polish fronts collapse
Tukhachevsky's Western Front begins an all-out assault in Belarus and reaches Białystok on 28 July
Piłsudski conceives a revised plan at the Belweder Palace on the night of 5 to 6 August
The final Soviet assault on Warsaw begins on 12 August with the attack on the Praga bridgehead and at Radzymin
Piłsudski's Task Force begins its march north from the Wieprz River on 16 August
The Polish army defeats the Red Army again at the Battle of the Niemen River, fought from 15 to 21 September
A ceasefire is signed on 12 October under pressure from France and Britain, and the fighting ends by 18 October
The Treaty of Riga, signed on 18 March, ends hostilities

sections.background:
Poland regained its independence after the partitions of 1795 and, after the First World War, fought to keep it and to shape the borders of a new multinational federation, called Intermarium, from the territories of its former partitioners Russia, Germany and Austria. In 1919 the Bolsheviks gained the upper hand in the Russian Civil War. Lenin viewed Poland as a bridge to bring communism to central and western Europe, and Bolshevik speeches asserted that the revolution would be carried west on the bayonets of Russian soldiers and that the shortest route to Berlin and Paris lay through Warsaw.

Józef Piłsudski, the Polish head of state, formed an alliance with the Ukrainian leader Symon Petlyura on 21 April 1920, and their forces pushed into Ukraine, entering Kiev on 7 May. A Red Army counter-offensive then nullified the Polish Kiev Operation. Semyon Budyonny's 1st Cavalry Army broke through the Polish lines in early June, and all Polish fronts collapsed.

On 4 July Mikhail Tukhachevsky's Western Front began an all-out assault in Belarus from the Berezina River. The Red Army seized Grodno on 19 July, captured the Brześć Fortress on 22 July and reached Białystok on 28 July. Polish and Soviet delegations met at Baranavichy in early August, but the talks came to nothing. By mid-1920 foreign observers expected Poland to collapse at any moment. The Bolsheviks expected the fall of Warsaw to spark communist uprisings and to clear the way for the Red Army to join the German Revolution.
sections.forces:
The Polish order of battle lists three fronts, seven armies and 32 divisions: 46,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry, 730 machine guns, 192 artillery batteries and several units of tanks, mostly FT-17. The army was newly created and its rifles and artillery were made in at least six countries, each using different ammunition. Piłsudski remarked that in the 21st Division almost half the soldiers who paraded before him were barefoot.

Piłsudski's plan, worked out on the night of 5 to 6 August, called for the Poles to withdraw across the Vistula and hold the bridgeheads at Warsaw and on the Wieprz. The 1st and 2nd Armies were to hold their entrenched positions in front of Warsaw at all costs, and the 5th Army under General Władysław Sikorski was to defend the Modlin area and strike when it could. The crucial role went to a newly formed Task Force of about 20,000 men under Piłsudski, drawn from the best units of the southern front and reinforced by the 4th and 3rd Armies. It was to strike north from the Vistula–Wieprz triangle at a weak spot between the Soviet Western and Southwestern Fronts, held only by the weak Mozyr Group, and meet the 5th Army near the East Prussian border.

Tukhachevsky planned to cross the Vistula near Włocławek, northwest of Warsaw, and attack the capital from that direction, repeating Ivan Paskevich's manoeuvre of 1831 and cutting the Poles off from Gdańsk, the only port open to arms and supplies. His weakness was the southern flank, covered only by the Pinsk Marshes and the Mozyr Group, whose 57th Infantry Division had 8,000 men.
sections.course:
The final Soviet assault began on 12 August. The 16th Army attacked at Radzymin, 23 kilometres east of Warsaw, and the Praga bridgehead came under frontal assault. Radzymin changed hands several times. The Polish 5th Army had to fight three Soviet armies at once and its lines were broken, but around midnight the 203rd Uhlan Regiment broke through and destroyed a radio station of the Soviet 4th Army. Polish operators jammed the remaining one, and the army marched on toward Toruń and Płock, unaware of Tukhachevsky's order to turn south. The 5th Army counterattacked across the Wkra River on 14 August. On 15 August the Soviet advance was halted and Radzymin was retaken. The closest any Soviet unit came was Izabelin, 13 kilometres northwest of the capital.

Budyonny's 1st Cavalry Army disobeyed the order to advance on Warsaw from the south and marched on Lwów instead. On 16 August Piłsudski's Task Force marched north from the Wieprz against the Mozyr Group, which had been reduced to one or two divisions on a 150-kilometre front. Only one of five Polish divisions met any opposition, and four advanced 45 kilometres unopposed, cutting the supply lines of the Soviet 16th Army.

On 18 August Tukhachevsky, at Minsk, ordered a retreat, but his orders came too late or not at all. The Polish 1st Legions Infantry Division marched 262 kilometres from Lubartów to Białystok in six days and cut off the 16th Army, most of whose troops surrendered. The 15th Army was defeated on 19 and 20 August, and by 21 August all organised resistance had ceased.
sections.aftermath:
Piłsudski's plan to surround the Red Army did not succeed completely. Of the four Soviet armies that advanced on Warsaw, the 4th, 15th and 16th, with most of Bzhishkyan's 3rd Cavalry Corps, all but disintegrated, their remnants taken prisoner or interned after crossing into German East Prussia. The 3rd Army was least affected, since its speed of retreat kept the Polish pursuers from catching it. Between 25,000 and 30,000 Soviet troops reached the German border and, after brief internment, were allowed to leave with their arms and equipment.

Red Army losses are put at about 15,000 dead, 500 missing, 10,000 wounded and 65,000 captured, or at 10,000 killed, 500 missing, 30,000 wounded and 66,000 taken prisoner. Polish losses are some 4,500 killed, 22,000 wounded and 10,000 missing. Poland captured about 231 pieces of artillery and 1,023 machine guns. Budyonny's army, besieging Lwów, was beaten at Komarów on 31 August and at Hrubieszów.

Tukhachevsky reorganised his retreating forces and set up a new defensive line near Grodno in September, but the Poles defeated him again at the Niemen River from 15 to 21 September. After the Battle of the Szczara River both sides were exhausted. A ceasefire was signed on 12 October under heavy pressure from France and Britain, the fighting was over by 18 October, and the Treaty of Riga of 18 March 1921 ended hostilities. The Polish victory also forced the cancellation of the Soviet attempt to overthrow the government of Lithuania, planned for August.
sections.sources:
The Polish plan is known through the memoirs of its makers and the reports written afterwards. Piłsudski admitted in his memoirs that it was a gamble, and General Maxime Weygand wrote in his that the victory, the plan and the army were Polish. Its authorship was nevertheless disputed. After the battle many reports credited Weygand or the Polish chief of staff Tadeusz Jordan-Rozwadowski, and Paderewski told Allied leaders that Weygand had the idea. According to recent research, the French mission proposed only a minor counter-attack by two divisions towards Mińsk Mazowiecki, Rozwadowski a deeper thrust from the Wieprz, and Piłsudski a large-scale operation. Davies describes the order as issued on the evening of 6 August after Piłsudski and Rozwadowski worked out the details. The Soviets are said to have intercepted a copy of the plan and discarded it as a poor deception.

On the Soviet side the dispute is over blame. Tukhachevsky blamed Stalin, who as political commissar of the South-Western Front aimed at Lwów, and Lenin and Trotsky blamed Stalin too. Stalin's secretary Boris Bazhanov argued that the offensive failed because Stalin and his army ignored the commander in chief's orders. In 1973 Thomas Fiddick judged rumours of disobedience by Budyonny or Stalin baseless, but more recent historians say Stalin did disobey. Davies argues that the Soviets were slow to bring forces up and poorly coordinated. Documents found in 2005 in Poland's Central Military Archives show that Polish cryptanalysts had broken Russian ciphers as early as September 1919.
sections.legacy:
Lenin called the result "an enormous defeat" for the Red Army. The Treaty of Riga secured the Polish state's eastern frontiers until 1939. The politician and diplomat Edgar Vincent regards the battle as one of the most important in history, since the Polish victory halted the spread of communism further west. In his view a Soviet victory would have led to a Soviet-established government in Poland and put the Soviets directly on the German border, where they were expecting or had been promised aligned forces.

The name "Miracle on the Vistula" was coined by the National Democrat deputy Stanisław Stroński to underline his disapproval of Piłsudski's earlier Ukrainian adventure. Prime Minister Wincenty Witos answered that whatever one wrote and whomever one dressed in laurels, this was the 1920 Miracle on the Vistula. Diaries of many participants attribute the outcome to the Blessed Virgin Mary, citing widespread national prayer beforehand and later reports of her appearance on the battlefield. The turn of the battle, 15 August, is the feast of the Assumption, an important date in the Catholic year.

For many years a myth persisted that the arrival of Allied forces had saved Poland, with Weygand at its centre. The raid of the 203rd Uhlans is sometimes called the Miracle of Ciechanów. Lieutenant Jan Kowalewski, credited with the original breakthrough in breaking Russian ciphers, received the Order of Virtuti Militari in 1921.

summary: In August 1920 Soviet armies under Tukhachevsky reached the approaches to Warsaw, where a Polish counterattack from the south led by Piłsudski broke their offensive and sent them eastward in disorder. The Treaty of Riga of 1921 then fixed Poland's eastern frontier.
notes: Loss figures: the article gives two sets for the Red Army (lead: 10,000 killed, 500 missing, 30,000 wounded, 66,000 captured; aftermath: 15,000 dead, 500 missing, 10,000 wounded, 65,000 captured). Both are given in the aftermath; the takeaway uses the second set. Polish figures agree in both places.

Radzymin: the article says the 16th Army captured it on the day after 12 August (13th), then that it fell on 14 August, then that it was retaken on 15 August. I wrote only that it changed hands several times and was retaken on 15 August.
Haller is called commander of the Central Front in the plan and of the Northern Front in the battle narrative; I left his name out.
The Soviet order of battle section of the article is empty; only Tukhachevsky's 24 divisions in four armies are given.
The date: the lead says only 'August 1920'; 12 August (final assault) and 16 August (counterattack) are the article's own dates. Span left as 'August 1920'.

The article contains 'Blitzkrieg-like', 'amateurish', and praise of the lead 'decisive Polish victory' and 'complete disintegration'; I used neither the lead's words nor Blitzkrieg. The 'amateurish' remark is attributed to officers and advisers.
The article says the Soviet 4th Army 'continued marching toward Toruń and Płock'; kept as given.

Left out: Piłsudski's letter of resignation, Nasielsk detail beyond 'nearly destroyed', the Mazyr Group's earlier Kiev role, the Ukrainian Army and 6th Army at Lwów, Edgar Vincent's counterfactual beyond his attributed view (kept, attributed).
